text: A real production pipeline isn't one script that does everything at once — it's a chain of gates. Build, test, scan, deploy, each one asking the same question: is there any reason not to ship this change? If the answer is yes, the pipeline stops right there, before wasting time on whatever comes next. That ordering is the whole design.

Build turns source into something deployable, usually a container image tagged with the commit SHA, and it should fail fast on anything that makes the artifact itself invalid. Test runs in two tiers: unit tests check code in isolation, fast enough for every commit, while integration tests spin the artifact up against a real database or queue and catch the bugs that only show up when pieces actually interact. Scan is where security plugs in directly. Deploy, in a GitOps setup, doesn't touch the cluster at all — it updates the GitOps repo, and ArgoCD or Flux reconciles the rest.

The scan stage is really four different checks stacked together. SAST tools like Semgrep analyze the code your team wrote for insecure patterns. SCA — software composition analysis — checks every third-party dependency against known CVE databases, the same alerts you saw from Dependabot back in the DevSecOps course. Secrets detection, with a tool like gitleaks, catches credentials accidentally committed into the diff or the history. And IaC scanning, with Checkov or tfsec, catches misconfigured Terraform or Kubernetes manifests before they're ever applied. Any one of these failing is just as valid a reason to stop as a failed test.

Here's that gate chain in real YAML. Each job declares needs on the one before it — test needs build, scan needs test, deploy needs scan — and that's a hard dependency, not a suggestion. GitHub Actions literally will not start the deploy job until scan reports success. Deploy's own steps don't SSH anywhere; they edit an image tag in the GitOps repo and push the commit, leaving the actual cluster change to the pull-based controller that's already watching that repo.

Once that commit lands and the GitOps controller picks it up, the next real question is how the new version actually reaches live traffic — all at once, or gradually. That's canary and blue-green deployments, coming up next.
